In other words, they are not fully conscious of what they are doing.
Conversely, a person who lacks this self-awareness does not ask why they think and say what they think and say. What they say can therefore only be opinion or ideology.

But if I know that my opinion or ideology is merely an opinion or ideology—and therefore not knowledge—then by that very fact it is no longer simply an opinion or ideology. It has become knowledge of an opinion or ideology.
I may still not know what knowledge itself is, but I do know that my opinion is not knowledge. I know that it is an opinion.

The contents of a precommunist Phenomenology therefore retain an “ideological” colouring.

But systematic philosophy in turn presupposes the truth of Phenomenology.
So once again we have a “circle.”

142) What is at issue here is the theory of knowledge—gnoseology—meaning the study of knowledge in the true sense, or, put differently, of convincing discourse.
Our claim is that this kind of study is impossible if knowledge is separated from reality.

It is possible, however, to study discourse while setting aside its power to convince. So-called “formal” logic, for example, studies discourse from the standpoint of its consistency, and therefore asks whether it is meaningful and coherent.
Grammar, in turn, sets consistency aside and studies the articulated structure of discourse.

Etymology studies the independently functioning elements that make up discourse—its “links,” or words. Syntax studies meaningful combinations of words without asking whether they contain a “logical” contradiction.
Syntax therefore accepts the grammatical correctness of a sentence such as “the black rectangular circle is white,” while rejecting a collection of words such as “he to the house do from always.”
So it can appear that logic and grammar study discourse independently of its relation to reality—independently of its “content,” that is, without asking whether the discourse is knowledge or not.
In reality, however, this is an illusion. But we cannot discuss that question here.

144) In his Phenomenology, Hegel studies both aspects at the same time.

His extraordinary stylistic ability enabled him to write the book in such a way that almost every sentence simultaneously describes—depending on how it is interpreted—both a stage in the development of knowledge as it reveals reality and an element of the reality revealed at that stage of knowledge.
Moreover, this aspect of reality is described simultaneously on both the ontological and the cosmological level. The meaning of these terms will be explained later.
Hegel’s Phenomenology therefore does more than prepare the possibility of knowledge. It also supplies the material needed to realize that knowledge in systematic philosophy.
But this method of presentation makes the book practically unreadable—or at the very least extremely difficult to understand.
I have therefore separated the two aspects.

And because a clear and broadly accessible presentation of the second aspect would have at least doubled the length of this already substantial book, I decided not to present the side concerning reality here.
Admittedly, in the systematic part I will therefore have to reconstruct the real aspect corresponding to each stage.
Still, it seems to me that this procedure will make both the Phenomenology itself and the logic of the Cosmology easier to understand.
Unfortunately, I have not managed to eliminate the real aspect completely. In other words, my Phenomenology is not perfectly uniform.

He likewise does not separate form from content. He does not show us “cognition in general,” but the actual knowledge of the world and of humanity achieved by a concrete human being.
Plato’s theory of knowledge, however, is not historical.
The opinions he examines exist alongside one another, but they do not emerge from one another.
His theory of knowledge is therefore not “systematic”: it gives no guarantee that it is exhaustive, and it does not show why the opinions it studies necessarily arise, change, and disappear.

The question of “races” therefore belongs to systematic philosophy—to Cosmology—whereas the question of “racist” theories belongs to Phenomenology.
